questions.prompt: Which statement about horizontal gene transfer is FALSE?

options.text: Plasmids carry accessory genes separate from the chromosome.
It is what makes genetic engineering of bacteria possible.
It passes genetic information within a generation.
It is how humans pass genes to their children.
Bacteria can exchange plasmid copies with neighbors.

questions.explanation: False. Parent-to-child inheritance is vertical gene transfer.

questions.prompt: A restriction enzyme that recognizes GAATTC makes a staggered cut. What does this produce?

options.text: Primers
Blunt ends
Sticky ends
Okazaki fragments

questions.explanation: The zigzag cut leaves single-stranded overhangs (sticky ends) that pair with complementary overhangs.

questions.prompt: Why did Paul Berg cut both viral DNAs with the same restriction enzyme?

options.text: To make the DNA single-stranded
Because only one restriction enzyme existed
So the pieces would have matching sticky ends that could join
To destroy the cancer-causing genes

questions.explanation: Same enzyme → complementary sticky ends, which ligase can then seal together.

questions.prompt: What did Paul Berg refuse to do with his recombinant DNA, and why?
questions.explanation: He refused to put it into E. coli. It contained DNA from SV40 (which causes cancer in monkeys), and E. coli is common in the human gut — if it escaped the lab, it could pose a cancer risk to humans. He thought it was simply too soon.

questions.prompt: How did Boyer's team create a gene for human insulin to put in bacteria?

options.text: Used PCR on human pancreas cells
Cut it out of a pig chromosome
Worked backward from insulin's amino-acid sequence to a DNA sequence and synthesized it
Used CRISPR to edit E. coli's own genes

questions.explanation: Knowing insulin's primary structure, they reversed the central dogma (protein → mRNA → DNA) and built a synthetic gene.

questions.prompt: Which PCR step occurs at about 55 °C?

options.text: Denaturation
Extension
Annealing (priming)
Ligation

questions.prompt: Why is Taq polymerase used in PCR instead of a typical bacterial DNA polymerase?

options.text: It works at room temperature
It doesn't need primers
It is thermostable and survives the high denaturation temperatures
It copies RNA into DNA

questions.explanation: Taq comes from the thermophile Thermus aquaticus, so it doesn't denature at near-boiling temperatures.

questions.prompt: Which statement about PCR is FALSE?

options.text: Helicase, primase, and ligase must be added to the tube.
Primers flank the region to be copied.
The number of target copies increases exponentially.
It amplifies a specific region of DNA.
A thermal cycler automates the temperature changes.

questions.explanation: False. Heat does helicase's job, synthetic primers replace primase, and ligase isn't needed; DNA polymerase is the only enzyme added.

questions.prompt: Explain how a PCR test gives a positive versus a negative result for a pathogen.
questions.explanation: Primers are designed to match a sequence unique to the pathogen. If the pathogen's DNA is in the sample, the primers bind and the region is amplified over many cycles → positive. If it isn't, the primers have nothing to bind, nothing is amplified → negative.

questions.prompt: What determines where Cas9 cuts DNA?

options.text: The ~20-nucleotide target sequence of its guide RNA
A palindromic recognition sequence built into Cas9
The promoter of the gene
Random chance

questions.explanation: The guide RNA base-pairs with matching DNA; swapping guide RNAs reprograms Cas9.

questions.prompt: A researcher wants to replace a faulty gene sequence with a correct one using CRISPR. What must be supplied along with Cas9 and guide RNA?

options.text: Donor DNA with ends matching the cut site
DNA ligase
Taq polymerase
A restriction enzyme

questions.explanation: Donor DNA tricks the cell into homology-directed repair, copying the corrected sequence in (knock-in).

questions.prompt: If a cell repairs a Cas9 cut by non-homologous end joining, what usually happens to the gene?

options.text: It is transcribed more often
It is knocked out (inactivated) by a mutation
It is corrected
It is copied onto a plasmid

questions.explanation: Random nucleotides are glued in, introducing a mutation that usually ruins the gene.

questions.prompt: Why is cystic fibrosis hard to treat with CRISPR in an adult patient?

options.text: Every cell carries the faulty gene, so Cas9 would need to reach essentially all of them
CRISPR can't cut human DNA
Cystic fibrosis is caused by a virus
The CFTR gene is on a plasmid

questions.explanation: It's inherited, so it's in every cell; correcting it is far easier in a fertilized egg/embryo.

questions.prompt: Which pair discovered CRISPR gene editing (Nobel 2020)?

options.text: Watson & Crick
Doudna & Charpentier
Hershey & Chase
Cohen & Boyer

questions.prompt: What is germline gene editing, and what is currently allowed for human embryos?
questions.explanation: Editing sperm, eggs, or embryos so the change is in every cell and is passed to future generations. Research on human embryos and germ cells is supported (NAS, 2017), but edited embryos may not be implanted — no CRISPR babies.

questions.prompt: Which statement about CRISPR is FALSE?

options.text: It has been used to treat sickle cell disease in an adult patient.
It is naturally an immune system in bacteria.
It defends bacteria against bacteriophage DNA.
It can be used to knock genes in or out.
CRISPR-edited foods must be labeled as GMOs.

questions.explanation: False. Editing (turning genes on/off) isn't classed as a GMO, so CRISPR-edited foods don't have to be labeled.
